discount codes
for your school to receive the special discounted rate.

Student Rush – Half Price Seats!

Starting
2 hours
before every performance, students with valid school ID can go to the Benedum Center Box Office and purchase up to two tickets for any available seats for half price.

Get a Group Together for Special Discounts

Groups of 6 or more students, faculty, and staff can get great group prices and all the benefits of traditional groups. Contact
Álvaro Muñoz
for more information.

Other Student Discounts

Students in grades K-12 are eligible for half-price children’s tickets.

text:
BRAVO! Champions of Music Education
In this ever-changing climate, music education can be a powerful tool for building community, encouraging self-expression, and fostering resilience. This season, the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra will recognize champions in music education who provide high quality music learning opportunities and broad access to students throughout the region. This includes the essential behind-the-scenes advocates who create school schedules, safe spaces, creative environments, and seamless logistics that enable students to flourish.
This new program,
BRAVO! Champions for Music Education
, will turn the spotlight on individuals in various roles who work to promote music learning in school-based music programs for PreK through 12th grade students.
Nominate a Music Educator
Please join us in celebrating this year’s Champions of Music Education!
2026-27 Honorees
Katie Black
Orchestra Director, Butler Senior High & Intermediate High School, Butler Area School District
Katie Black is an orchestra educator and violinist who believes music has the power to create community, build confidence, and give students a place to belong. She has taught in the Butler Area School District since 2015, working with students in grades 6–12. She is the founder and director of Butler Rock Orchestra, an audition-based group that takes classical strings and combines rock elements. Under her direction, the ensemble has performed throughout the region, including at the PMEA State Conference in 2020 and 2024, various elementary tours, and last December performed a sold out show in collaboration with Cello Fury at the historic Penn Theater in Butler.
Katie is passionate about creating meaningful opportunities for students to perform, lead, and find their own voice through music. She also performs throughout the region as a professional violinist and fiddler with The Jive Daisy and other musical projects. She holds a Bachelor of Music Education from Seton Hill University. Above all, Katie believes music brings people together and creates meaningful memories and experiences that can shape students for years to come.
Karen Bottegal
Music Teacher, Pittsburgh Montessori PreK-5, Pittsburgh Public Schools
I am an elementary general music teacher with Pittsburgh Public Schools, currently teaching at Pittsburgh Montessori PreK-5. I believe music education is about so much more than learning to sing, play an instrument, or read music. Music can help students discover who they are and find a place where they belong. It gives them opportunities to express themselves, connect with others, build confidence, and experience the joy of creating something together.
I also believe music brings joy to education. For some students, music class is the place where they feel most successful, most comfortable being themselves, or simply most excited to come to school. I love watching students discover something in music that becomes theirs, whether that is singing, playing an instrument, composing, moving, performing, or just realizing that they are a musician.
One of the most important parts of my work is making sure those experiences are available to every child. I want my students to leave elementary school knowing that music is something they can participate in, enjoy, and carry with them, wherever their lives take them.
Eryn Carranza
Band Director, South Fayette High School and Intermediate School, South Fayette Twp. School District
Eryn Carranza began her tenure with the South Fayette Township School District in 2007 and has served as Director of Bands at South Fayette High School since 2011. In this role, she conducts the marching band, concert bands, pep band, pit orchestra, percussion ensemble, and, most recently, the jazz ensemble. She also teaches at South Fayette Intermediate School, where she directs the Beginning Band and 5th Grade Band, giving her the unique opportunity to work with students from their very first experiences as instrumental musicians through their high school years.
From 2019 through 2025, Eryn had the honor of serving the members of District 1 of the Pennsylvania Music Educators Association (PMEA), including as District President from 2021 to 2023. During a period marked by the challenges of the pandemic, she helped reestablish in-person PMEA events, establish a mini-grant program to support music education throughout the district, and strengthen connections among music educators across the region.
Eryn continues to perform on her primary instrument, tuba, with community ensembles including the Allegheny Brass Band and West Hills Symphonic Band. She is also a proud two-time member of the Saluting America’s Band Directors Marching Band, performing in both the Rose Parade and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
Eryn believes music is at the core of who we are as human beings. It is an essential part of our culture and our humanity, with a remarkable power to unite people across generations, cultures, and differences. Music can make us rejoice, make us weep, and help us express what words alone cannot. In a world that continues to yearn for peace, music and the arts offer hope for greater unity, acceptance, and understanding.
So many of the people who have shaped Eryn’s life are in it because of music education. Her hope is to provide that same gift to her students—not only by teaching them to become musicians, but by creating a place where they feel safe, where they belong, where they are valued and loved, and where they are free to become the truest versions of themselves.
Jason Cheskawich
Music Educator, Mellon Middle School, Mt. Lebanon School District
Jason Cheskawich has been teaching in the Mt. Lebanon School District since 2010, spending most of his time at the high school directing concert, jazz, and marching ensembles. He currently teaches bands at Mellon Middle School.
Throughout his career, Jason has been fortunate to prepare students to perform on remarkable stages, including PMEA Annual In-Service Conferences, the PMEA/NAfME Eastern Division Conference, and the Music for All National Festival. He earned his Bachelor of Music degree from Duquesne University in 1998, where he studied trumpet with George Vosburgh and conducting with Dr. Robert Cameron.
For Jason, the most meaningful part of music education is helping students grow—not only as musicians, but as people. He believes music has a unique ability to bring people together and create experiences that stay with them their entire lives. Jason lives in Mt. Lebanon with his wife, Amanda, a fellow Mt. Lebanon music educator, and their three children, Lilly, Carson, and Emma.
Mairi Cooper
Orchestra Director, Fox Chapel Area High School, Fox Chapel Area School District
Mairi Cooper has been a music teacher and orchestra director at Fox Chapel Area High School for the past 25 years. Under Mairi’s leadership, the Fox Chapel Area High School music program was the first public school recognized as an “Exemplary Program” by the Middle States Accreditation Committee. In 2015-16, Mairi was honored to have served as the Pennsylvania Teacher of the Year.
Mairi is an ardent advocate of public education, believing that it is an imperative to offer quality education to every child. She is passionate about the importance of educating the whole child and believes that all children should receive an education that both interests and challenges them. She believes strongly that creativity in children must be nurtured and developed. A quality education always includes the arts.
Mairi has received numerous awards for her teaching including Pennsylvania/Delaware String Teachers Association Outstanding New Orchestra Teacher Award, the Yale University Distinguished Music Educator Award, and the Carson Scholar “Power of Excellence.” Mairi’s proudest moments have occurred when her students have used music as a change agent within the Pittsburgh community, sharing their talents to better other’s lives.
Sean Desguin
Elementary Band Director; Central, Poff, and Wyland Elementary Schools, Hampton Middle School; Hampton Township School District
I am in my 25th year teaching, having spent the past 20 years as Elementary Band Director in the Hampton Township School District. I also serve as Assistant Director of the Hampton Middle School and Hampton High School Marching Bands. Since 2006, I have been Associate Conductor of the North Pittsburgh Symphonic Band, a community ensemble based in the north hills of Pittsburgh. I believe in the power of music education to build creativity, teamwork, and perseverance!
Becky Dougan
General Music and Chorus Teacher, Pittsburgh Dilworth PreK-5, Pittsburgh Public Schools
I’m grateful to have been a music teacher for 33 years, the last 23 in Pittsburgh Public Schools. I believe that music education provides children with opportunities to grow in artistic skill and creativity, but also connect with their humanity and that of their school, city, and world communities.
Gretchen Eckroat
Music Teacher, Pittsburgh Concord, Pittsburgh Public Schools
A dedicated educator with 29 years of teaching experience, this Pittsburgh native and Pittsburgh Public Schools graduate earned a degree in Music Education from Mansfield University of Pennsylvania and holds certifications in all three levels of Orff Schulwerk. After launching a teaching career with three years in Prince George’s County, Maryland, I returned home to Pittsburgh Public Schools, where I have been inspiring young musicians for the past 26 years. Throughout my career, I have taught middle school general music, elementary general music, and beginning instrumental music, while actively shaping the district’s musical community by co-founding the Pittsburgh Public Schools Sing Program and helping with the All City Music program.
Mariann Fox
Elementary Vocal Music Teacher, Markham & Foster Elementary Schools, Mt. Lebanon
Mariann is beginning her 35th year as a music educator, with the past 14 years spent teaching elementary music in the Mt. Lebanon School District outside of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. During her time in Mt. Lebanon, she has also had the opportunity to serve as the Supervisor of Fine Arts and Health and Physical Education.
Mariann began her teaching career in her alma mater, the Aliquippa School District, before continuing her work in the Quaker Valley School District and ultimately joining the Mt. Lebanon School District. For the past two years, she has also served as an Ambassador for the QuaverEd Music program.
Music has always been an important part of Mariann’s life. It has provided her with a meaningful outlet for creativity and a lifelong passion for performance—one that naturally grew into a desire to share the joy and power of music with children. After 35 years in education, that passion continues to inspire her work and the students she serves.
Deanna Grandstaff
Band Director, Cecil Intermediate School, Canon-McMillan School District
Music has been a meaningful part of my life for as long as I can remember, and becoming a music educator has allowed me to share that passion with others. I have been fortunate to serve the children of the Canon-McMillan School District since 2007. I teach 5th and 6th grade band at Cecil Intermediate School and 4th grade band at Muse Elementary School.
I earned a Bachelor’s degree in Music Education from Penn State University and a Master of Education in Teaching and Leadership from Point Park University. I am the second music educator to earn a Pennsylvania Endorsement in Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Management of PK-12 Students.
I serve on the Recording Academy’s national Music Education and Professional Development Committee. I am the only recipient of the Country Music Association Foundation’s Music Teachers of Excellence Award from Pennsylvania. I have been a Quarterfinalist for the Grammy Music Educator Award in 2027, 2026, 2024, and 2023.
I believe music education is about much more than learning to play an instrument or perform a piece of music. Music provides students with opportunities to develop confidence, creativity, perseverance, collaboration, and a sense of belonging. I am especially passionate about creating an inclusive environment where every student has the opportunity to experience the benefits of music, regardless of physical limitations, cognitive disabilities, or socioeconomic circumstances.
Music is important to me because it has the unique ability to connect people. It can communicate emotions and experiences when words are not enough, bring people from different backgrounds together, and create lasting memories. I have seen firsthand how music can help students discover strengths they did not know they possessed and find a place where they feel successful and valued.
I hope to continue helping students experience the joy, connection, and lifelong impact that music has brought to my own life.
Tom Koharchik
Choir Director, Freeport Area High School and Middle School, Freeport Area School District
I have been the choir director at Freeport Area Middle and High Schools since 2006. In that position, I direct the 6th grade chorus, 7/8th grade chorus, and high school concert choir. I also teach music technology and produce/direct two high school musicals and one middle school musical each year. I am also the PMEA District 3 Treasurer and Secretary, the Freeport High School Key Club Advisor, Jr. Class Sponsor, Tri-M Advisor, and Yearbook Business Manager. I earned my BS in Music Education from Indiana University of Pennsylvania in 2003 and my Masters in Music Education from Duquesne University in 2014.
I believe music education is extremely important in order to foster an outlet for self-expression and belonging in our schools. It allows students to process complex emotions and discover their own unique identities in ways that no other subject can. It teaches students self-discipline, resilience, and patience. Music education also helps to bridge cultural and social divides by uniting diverse groups of people through a language of creativity and shared human experience.
Len Lavelle
Band Director and Curriculum Leader, North Hills High School, North Hills School District
Len is in his 25th year of teaching and currently serves as the High School Band Director and Music Department Curriculum Leader at North Hills.
Not coming from a musical family, he remembers the impact of attending student outreach events through the PSO in high school. He went on to study with members of the orchestra and the PSO has remained an important part of his life.
Len still teaches music today because he has seen the power of a quality music education and ensemble music to change students' lives in ways that nothing else can.
He remains grateful for arts in Greater Pittsburgh, the North Hills music community, his administrators who value music education in our students' lives, the thousands of amazing students he has learned music with over the years, his inspiring and supportive colleagues, and, most importantly, his family Sarah (violin), Grace (clarinet/piano/voice), and Annie (horn/voice).
Thank you to the PSO for the honor of being here with you tonight and for choosing to make a difference through music.
Sarah Lavelle
Orchestra Teacher, North Allegheny Senior High School, North Allegheny School District
I started my career in the Beaver Area School District, and I've been teaching in the North Allegheny School District since 2006. I teach string orchestra classes at North Allegheny Intermediate and Senior High Schools.
I get to work with incredible students every day, and I love watching them grow as musicians over their high school years. I became a music teacher because of the incredible teachers I had growing up and because of the impact music had on my life; I strive to give my students the same experiences and hope music enriches their lives as well.
Marissa McFarren
Band Director, Brownsville Area Schools, Brownsville Area School District
I am now in my fifth year of building the music program at Brownsville, and it has been a true privilege to watch it grow. What began with just 13 students has developed into a thriving music department with multiple ensembles, awards, and meaningful opportunities for students of all abilities and backgrounds.
There is an indescribable joy in creating the same memorable, life-shaping experiences for our students that we once experienced ourselves—experiences that inspired us to become educators and ultimately led us here. Watching our students discover that same joy through music is one of the most rewarding parts of what we do!
Keegan McLean
Director of Bands, Redbank Valley Intermediate and High School, Redbank Valley School District
Sharing music is important with others because it is one of the few innate subjects that surrounds us our entire lives. I was lucky enough to have many inspirational music teachers at Plum Senior High and want to provide that experience for my students.
Katie Miller
Music Teacher, Dickson Preparatory STEAM Academy, Woodland Hills School District
I have dedicated over 20 years to serving the Woodland Hills School District through music education and currently teach 6th grade Chorus and 7th & 8th grade General Music at Dickson Preparatory STEAM Academy. I’ve been part of the Woodland Hills Marching Band staff for 26 seasons and maintain a small private flute studio.
Throughout my career, I have been passionate about expanding access to meaningful arts experiences. From writing curriculum and directing ensembles to securing grants, hosting guest artists, and bringing organizations like the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra into our schools, I believe everyone deserves opportunities to experience the transformative power of the arts, regardless of their background or circumstances.
Kristy Ochs
Elementary General/Vocal Music Educator; Central, Mt. Vernon, and Greenock Elementary Schools; Elizabeth Forward School District
With over 25 years of experience teaching in a variety of schools, Kristy is a dedicated general and vocal elementary music educator with a deep passion for helping children discover the joy of music. As a certified Orff Schulwerk educator, Mrs. Ochs brings creativity, movement, singing, and hands-on musical experiences into the classroom, fostering an environment where every child can participate and succeed.
Kristy also serves on the Teacher Advisory Committee for the Pittsburgh Youth Chorus, contributing experience and insight to support young singers and music education in the community. Above all, Mrs. Ochs loves teaching children and believes that developing a love and appreciation for music at an early age can inspire a lifelong connection to the arts. Through joyful, engaging musical experiences, Kristy strives to help every child find their own voice and discover the power of music.
Michael Pagnotta
Director of Bands, Huston Middle School and Burrel Hill School, Burrell School District
Michael Pagnotta is a native of Edison, New Jersey, who relocated to Pittsburgh back in 2012. He enjoys all of what Pittsburgh has to offer with his wife and 3 wonderful children. Before moving to Pittsburgh, he was a musician and educator all around the country. As a lifelong fan of musical theater and a woodwind doubler, he has had the chance to perform as a pit musician in musical productions in Pittsburgh, New Hampshire, Phoenix, San Diego, and New York City, both on and off Broadway.
As an educator, Michael has founded 4 music programs in his career. 3 in Phoenix, AZ, and 1 in Pittsburgh. In Phoenix, founded a middle school choir program, a high school choir/theater program, and a 2-12 general music program. When he moved to Pittsburgh, he started another instrumental music program for students in grades K-3. Since 2014, Michael has been the director of bands for grades 5-12 in the Burrell School District. He is responsible for all levels of band and all types of bands within Burrell. The true highlight of his job is the opportunity to teach the same students for 8 years consecutively and collaborate with his fellow music educators, all of whom his job affords him the opportunity to spend quality alongside.
Music has always been a part of his life even though he does not come from a musical family. Michael knew at a very early age that he wanted to spend his life teaching music to others. He has always found that music and music classrooms were a place for self-expression, fun, and a collective weirdness that everyone seems to enjoy. Music tends to make everyone more equal since we all strive for the same goal: exceptional performance. Michael tries to bring that same fun energy and a safe space for all to his music classrooms now. It is his belief that music ties people together with an indescribable bond that everyone should experience within their lifetime. There is nothing quite like chasing the feeling of a round of applause for your hard work.
Finally, Michael would like to thank his parents for supporting his passion for music, his wife for her love and patience with all of his performing and the time that music education demands, his children for reminding him constantly that being fun and weird is the most important thing in life, his friends for their constant support and encouragement, and finally all of his colleagues and fellow performers. Those are the people who make what we do the most enjoyable part. Every pit musician and music educator he has met along the way has been someone worth spending time with, laughing with, and performing with. Thank you to everyone for recommending Michael for this recognition. He is flattered and honored beyond words.
Douglas Reichenfeld
Orchestra Director, Mt. Lebanon High School, Mt. Lebanon School District
Doug Reichenfeld proudly serves as the orchestra director at Mt. Lebanon High School, where he has taught music at all levels since 1998. As a third generation music educator, he seeks to instill a commitment to musical excellence in all of his students, as well as a lifelong love of the arts and music. Doug is grateful for the music education he recieved at the Oberlin Conservatory of Music, and for his early experiences as a trumpeter in PMEA, PYSO, and at the Pennsylvania Governor's School for the Arts.
Caroline Russell
Orchestra Director, Dutch Ridge Elementary, Beaver Area Middle School, Beaver Area High School, Beaver Area School District
I teach grades 4-12 orchestra at Beaver Area School District. I graduated from Duquesne University in 2021 with my B.S. in Music Education, and I will graduate from IUP with my M.A. in Music Education in December of 2026. I am a native violinist.
Music is important to me because of its ability to make us feel and push through. When you are teaching music to students, you aren't just teaching the technical aspects, you're teaching them how to express themselves. How to persevere. How to use critical thinking skills. How to problem solve. How to be independent. If I can help nurture one of those skills in a student and allow them to experience and express their emotions then I have done my job.
Rebecca Sensor
Choral Director/Music Instructor, DuBois Area Middle School, DuBois Area School District
Rebecca Sensor has taught music at DuBois Area Middle School since 2001. She teaches fifth-grade Rhythm and Movement, directs more than 300 students in the sixth- through eighth-grade choirs, leads the after-school theater program, and co-directs ukulele and modern band ensembles. Her previous roles include sixth-grade band director, middle school color guard instructor, and assistant high school marching band director. She currently chairs the DuBois Area School District Music and Performing Arts Department. The district has been recognized eight times as a NAMM Foundation Best Community for Music Education.
Rebecca earned a Bachelor of Arts in Music Education from Edinboro University of Pennsylvania and a Master of Education in Mid-Level Education and Curriculum from Walden University. An accomplished vocalist and flutist, she has performed at events across Pennsylvania. Her select choir performed in the Pennsylvania State Capitol Rotunda in 2009 and 2023. She has guest conducted numerous choral festivals, including PMEA District 3 Junior District Chorus, and will conduct the Rhode Island Music Education Association Elementary All-State Chorus in March.
Rebecca currently serves as President of the Pennsylvania Music Educators Association. Her previous PMEA leadership roles include District 3 President, Student Performance Events Council chair, and membership on several state committees and task forces. She has coordinated District 3 Chorus Fest since 2011, hosted numerous PMEA events, and co-hosted the 2019 All-State Chorus. She frequently presents professional development sessions at district, state, and national conferences and serves as a PMEA mentor, Model Curriculum Framework presenter, and modern band trainer.
A native of Somerset County, Rebecca credits her experiences in band, orchestra, and chorus at Somerset Area School District with inspiring her career in music education. She lives in Treasure Lake with her husband, Joe. Together, they raised their children, Max, Maddie, and Molly, and are now raising their nieces, Keti and Clara.
Christopher Snyder
Director of Bands, Deer Lakes High School, Deer Lakes School District
I have been the Director of Bands in the Deer Lakes School District since 2006. In that time, my responsibilities have included directing the 6th Grade Ensemble, the 7th & 8th Grade Concert Band, the High School Symphonic Band, the Deer Lakes Marching Band and the Deer Lakes Jazz Ensemble. In addition to my ensemble duties, I also teach a Fundamentals of Guitar class, Music Theory and Composition and a History of Rock & Roll class.
I am an active member of Pennsylvania Music Educators Association (PMEA), hold an executive position on the board of the Alle-Kiski Valley Band Directors Association (AKVBDA) and am the current President of the Pennsylvania Interscholastic Marching Band Association (PIMBA).
Chad Toporski
Music Teacher, Quaker Valley Middle School, Quaker Valley School District
Chad Toporski has served as the choral director and general music teacher at Quaker Valley Middle School since January 2025. Beyond the classroom, he serves as the producer and vocal director for the middle school musical, producer and pit conductor for the high school musical, and director of QV Harmony, the middle school contemporary a cappella ensemble. Previously, Chad taught in a similar capacity for 14 years at Hopewell Memorial Jr. High School in Beaver County.
An active member of the Pennsylvania Music Educators Association (PMEA) and National Association for Music Education (NAfME), Chad served four years as President of PMEA District 5 and on the PMEA State Board, championing expanded support for music educators, students, and programs. He continues to volunteer in PMEA District 1, advocating for equitable, high-quality music education at all levels. Chad firmly believes music is fundamental to our humanity—moving us emotionally, building community, and enriching our culture.
Aaron Taylor
Marching Band Director, Perry Traditional Academy 9-12, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Aaron Taylor is the marching band director at Perry Traditional Academy located in the North Side of Pittsburgh, Pa. Aaron is passionate about creating safe spaces for students to find and discover who they are in the arts. For the last 5 years, Aaron has successfully rebuilt the Perry Traditional Academy Marching Band. The Marching Band currently has 25 students who are passionate about striving to be the best they can be for each other and the marching band. During the month of May 2026, Aaron Taylor teamed up with Obama Academy 6 - 12 to travel down to Washington D.C. to march in the National Memorial Day Parade for America's 250th celebration. Aaron believes that music can open doors for all students: “We build the doors with the foundation of music which then allows the students access to walk through to a world of opportunities! Music is the key to allow students to become who they aspire to be.”
Nina Unitas
Senior Program Officer, Arts Education, Office of Curriculum & Instruction, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Music has always been a powerful force in my life, both personally and professionally. As an educator and arts advocate, I have seen firsthand how music can inspire, heal, and connect people across. Throughout my career in public education, I have supported music programs and worked alongside talented music educators who create transformative learning experiences for young people every day.
Music is important to me because it provides opportunities for creativity, emotional expression, and community building. Whether through performance, listening, or composition, music allows individuals to share their stories and deepen their understanding of others.
Shawn van Mastrigt
General Music/Musical Theater Director, Turner Intermediate School, Wilkinsburg School District
Shawn van Mastrigt is in his 32nd year teaching music in the Wilkinsburg School District. He began his career teaching high school choir and band, and now teaches at Turner Intermediate School, where his program is built on hands-on music making — African drumming, ukulele, choir, singing, and movement. A longtime participant in Carnegie Mellon University's Urban Music Education Program, he also founded and directs Turner's After-School Musical Theater program, now in its sixth year.
Shawn believes music belongs to everyone, not just the talented few, and he builds his program so that every student gets to perform. Stepping onto a stage asks something of them that little else does — courage, preparation, and trust in the people beside them. Students walk off changed by it. What he hopes they carry longest is simpler: a love of music and theater, woven into ordinary life.
2025-26 Honorees
Lucas Beaver
Band Director, North Hills School District
Lucas Beaver is a passionate educator dedicated to supporting and uplifting his students within and beyond the music classroom at North Hills High School. He firmly believes in establishing a culture of learning, responsibility, and both musical and personal growth in the band program and works closely with his orchestra and chorus colleagues along with the counselors, administrators, and faculty for the benefit of all involved. In addition to his position at North Hills, Lucas is the President of District 1 of the Pennsylvania Music Educators’ Association, advocating for quality music education and organizing inspirational music experiences for students across five counties.
Jesse Bush
Music Teacher, Serra Catholic High School
Jesse Bush is the high school music teacher at Serra Catholic High School. There, he directs the band, marching band, and the spring musical. Jesse takes on the challenge of giving every student in his music program — particularly the marching band program — a fantastic experience. He takes the marching band to perform at competitions and makes sure they are able to travel and have similar experiences as students in other, larger, marching bands. It’s clear to anyone who watches his students perform that they are enjoying their time in Jesse’s ensembles.
Marylou Monich Bushyager
Music Specialist, Pittsburgh Allegheny PreK-5, Pittsburgh King PreK-8, Pittsburgh Langley PreK-8, Pittsburgh Westwood PreK-5, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Marylou has been working as a music educator in the Pittsburgh Public Schools since January of 2004. She is a graduate of Slippery Rock University of Pennsylvania and holds a Bachelor of Science in Music Education (Saxophone) and a Master of Education in Special Education from Carlow University. She has taught high school choir, jazz ensemble, marching band, Middle School and Elementary instrumental music, modern band, and special music education. Her students have collaborated with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, Manchester Craftsman’s Guild, Pittsburgh Opera, Carnegie Mellon University, Urban Impact Foundation, PMEA, and performed at many community events throughout Pittsburgh. Her instrument group received a Superior rating at the High Note Music Festival at Duquesne University and recorded a music video with the Urban Music Education Project. Her philosophy is that music helps us grow in kindness, compassion, love, education, and helps us learn to thrive together in peace and harmony.
Robert Carr
Band Director, Woodland Hills High School
“In addition to serving as the daytime Band Director at Woodland Hills, I also direct our Marching Band, our Junior Musical, Assistant Direct our Spring Musical, and serve as a Performing Arts Workshop Instructor. I am extremely proud to teach at my alma mater and am thrilled to be able to help my wonderful students gain meaningful music experiences! They amaze me every day!”
Tina L. Esu
Music Specialist, Pittsburgh Faison, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Tina Esu is a Music Specialist at Pittsburgh Faison who has been working at Pittsburgh Public Schools since 1998. She goes above and beyond to help her students learn music in ways that truly resonate with them — using rhythm, the music they listen to at home, and connections with community partners to inspire learning and performance. Her collaborations with ChaRon Don have gone viral, showcasing original works that amplify student voices and celebrate their creativity. Whether her students are composing, performing, or diving into music literacy, Tina creates a space where they are engaged, confident, and thriving.
Sarah Giliberto
Music Educator, Pittsburgh Brookline PreK-8, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Sarah Giliberto has been teaching in the Pittsburgh Public Schools since February 2005. After spending 16 years teaching instrumental and vocal music at Carrick High School, she made a big career shift and moved to Brookline PreK-8 to instill a love of music in younger students. One of her favorite things to do is take her students to the Schooltime concerts at the PSO, especially when it’s their first trip to Heinz Hall. “I love how their little faces light up when they see the elegance of the hall and hear the beauty of the music. It makes everything worthwhile.” She is also only one of two music educators in her district with a National Board of Professional Teaching Standards Certification.
Stephanie Glover
Orchestra Director, Bethel Park High School, Bethel Park School District
Stephanie Glover is the orchestra director at Bethel Park High School. A tireless advocate for music education, she believes in nurturing lifelong musicians, and her students share her passion for playing and for the art form. Outside of her work at Bethel Park, where she has grown the orchestral program to a high level, she works extensively with students through TRYPO and PMEA, ensuring that young musicians can participate in high-quality and engaging ensembles.
Brian Lee
Music Director, Allderdice High School, Pittsburgh Public Schools
Brian Lee is the Music Director at Allderdice High School, where he leads vibrant ensembles who perform at marching festivals, PMEA events, and in the community. Beyond his instrumental work, Brian teaches one of the few AP Music Theory courses in the area along with choir and general music. He also regularly leads the pit orchestra in school musicals and accompanies his studies in cabaret performances. He is a powerful, witty, skilled musician and leader — we are lucky to have him work with our young people!
Dr. Kim Prentice
Coordinator, Performing Arts at the Pittsburgh Public Schools Office of Curriculum & Instruction
Dr. Kim Prentice serves as the Coordinator of Performing Arts for Pittsburgh Public Schools, supporting joyful, child-centered music learning across the city and advocating for equitable access to quality music education. Outside of the classroom, Kim enjoys competing in triathlon and traveling with family.
Jeanne Tupper
Orchestra Director & Music Teacher Grades 6–8, South Fayette Middle School, South Fayette Township School District
Jeanne Tupper is the Orchestra Director and Music Teacher at South Fayette Middle School. Since she started at South Fayette, she has grown their strings program by leaps and bounds. She teaches with sound pedagogical strategies and her students demonstrate consistent growth and improvement. She also volunteers her time to be the orchestra content representative to ensure consistency within the PMEA Orchestra festival system. In this role, she also sits on the statewide Student Performance Events Council.
Ronnie Ziccardi
Band Director, Avonworth School District
Ronnie’s teaching responsibilities at Avonworth include 3rd Grade General Music, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th/8th Grade Bands, Marching Band Assistant Director and Percussion Instructor, Middle School Jazz Band Director, and Director of the Musical Pit Orchestra. During his current 9-year tenure, the Avonworth elementary band program has expanded by about 6 times the number of involved students. The 6th-grade band participated in the PMEA Music Performance Assessment in 2023, 2024, and 2025 and has been awarded Superior Ratings (the highest rating possible) in all 3 performances.

text:
About the Trust

Performing Arts. Visual Arts. Festivals. Arts Education. Urban Development.
Since 1984, the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust
®
, a non-profit arts organization, has worked to make the Steel City a place where the arts can flourish. Our efforts have focused on the cultural and economic development of the Cultural District, a 14-square-block area of downtown Pittsburgh. What was once a downtrodden red light district now thrives as a vibrant center for culture, art, food, and community. Pittsburgh’s Cultural District stands as a nationwide model for how the arts can play a pivotal role in urban revitalization.
Each year, millions of people visit the Cultural District to expand their horizons in our theaters, galleries, and public art environments. Patrons enjoy thousands of
world-class performing arts events
and
visual arts exhibitions
. Pittsburgh residents of all ages connect and learn with the Trust’s
comprehensive education
and community engagement opportunities. Local arts organizations collaborate to build a stronger cultural community through the
power of partnerships
.

The Cultural District acts as the anchor for all of that work. The Trust’s
superior venues
and
gallery spaces
allow resident companies, community organizations, artists, and promoters to reach audiences large and small. In total, the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust manages more than
one million square feet of real estate
in the District. Step outside those buildings to find numerous
public art installations
that beautify Pittsburgh's largest arts neighborhood.

Lauded as “the single greatest creative force in Pittsburgh because of its spirit of reinvention” by the Pittsburgh Post Gazette, the Trust strives every day to enrich the city of Pittsburgh’s vibrancy, diversity, and prosperity.

Plan Your Visit

We’re so glad you decided to choose the Cultural District for your next arts adventure! Whether you’re new to this area or a frequent guest, we can’t wait to share the magic of live events with you.

The Cultural District is a project of the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust’s history. Dotted with theaters, restaurants, galleries, and public art, this neighborhood is home to Downtown’s dynamic arts, entertainment, and dining scene. Here, you’ll discover a spectrum of choices for entertainment, arts, and enlightenment including contemporary music, modern dance, visual art, and thought-provoking theater, as well as classical music, opera, ballet, popular musical theater, art film and more. You can find new and exciting things to do year-round in the Cultural District.

About the Harris Theater
The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust's Harris Theater is one of the most active arts facilities in the region showing art films nearly every day of the year.
Formerly known as the Art Cinema, the Harris Theater represents a milestone in the redevelopment of Liberty Avenue. The Art Cinema was the first moving picture house in Pittsburgh to commercially show art movies until competition from other city theaters led to its conversion to an adult movie house in the 1960s. As part of its mission to transform the Cultural District, the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust purchased and restored the facility leading to further conversions of run-down properties along the Liberty Avenue corridor. With a total of 194 seats, including a fully restored balcony, the Harris Theater officially opened to the public for movies and live performances on November 9, 1995. The theater is one of the few that has retained 35mm film projectors that are utilized regularly.
The Harris was named through a gift from the Buhl Foundation after John P. Harris, co-founder of the Nickelodeon—the first theater solely dedicated to the showing of motion pictures—and a Pennsylvania State Senator. The Harris Theater features contemporary, foreign, and classic films.

About Us

Choral performance like you’ve not seen before.

What We Do

Bach Choir of Pittsburgh (BCP) was founded in 1934 to perform works of Johann Sebastian Bach exclusively. Under the leadership of Conductor and Artistic Director Thomas W. Douglas, the choir continues to evolve from a narrowly-focused ensemble to a larger, more inclusive choir that performs major choral works by composers from the Renaissance through the present.

After its inception the Bach Choir grew from 60 to 100 singers, and it currently remains steady with 75 members, including a 16-person core of paid professional singers. BCP produces a three-production concert season that is presented in unique venues in and around Pittsburgh, in addition to a Summer Sing educational program in June of each year. Auditions for choir and professional core positions are held on an annual basis. In addition to our regular concert season, the Bach Choir is available
for hire
throughout the tri-state area.

The Choir is critically acclaimed for its innovative, precise, and entertaining concert performances. Local music critics commend the Choir for “stretching its musical wings,” and handling “tricky works not only with technical skill, but with spirit and seeming inspiration.” They praise Artistic Director Thomas W. Douglas as well. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette says “One has to admire Artistic Director and Conductor Thomas Douglas for thinking out of the proverbial box when it comes to choral music.” And the Tribune-Review raves, “Douglas is shaping the choir into a Pittsburgh musical force!”

Mission

The mission of the Bach Choir of Pittsburgh is to perform innovative choral music for arts-loving audiences by presenting unique artistic experiences drawn from a variety of musical genres and diverse cultural traditions
.

Vision

The Bach Choir of Pittsburgh will be a leading choral ensemble recognized for its offerings that surprise, delight and defy expectations.

Values

The Bach Choir of Pittsburgh values:

Diverse musical genres and cultural traditions

Excellence in musical technique and performance

Organizational and financial stability

Community engagement

Its audiences and patrons

Its donors, funders, volunteers and supporters

Collaboration with other artists

Partnerships with other arts organizations

Diversity in its membership, audience and leadership

Membership camaraderie

The talents of its membership

The talents of community composers, musicians, and performers

Audition and Membership

Join the BCP Family – Sing with the Bach Choir!

Auditions for the 26-27 season will be held on the evening of August 25, 2026. If you would like to audition, please fill out the form below.
The Auditions Coordinator will contact you to make arrangements for you to audition.

Questions regarding auditions should be sent to
auditions@bachchoirpittsburgh.org

The Bach Choir of Pittsburgh includes a core of professional, paid singers and also volunteer singers. The audition process for both categories are listed below. We welcome everyone to audition and are looking to diversify and expand our choir.

AUDITION PROCESS

Regular Member Auditions (5 Minutes in Length):

Sing one prepared piece (bring a copy of music for the accompanist)

Sight sing

Core Auditions (10 Minutes in Length):

Sing two memorized songs in two different languages.

(bring music for the accompanist)

Sight sing.

Oral testing (keys, chords, musical terms, etc.) and aural tests (scales, intervals, etc.) will also be part of your audition session

For singers whose are chosen to join the choir, an orientation session for new members will be held when rehearsals start in September. All choir members must re-audition for each season.

MEMBERSHIP INFORMATION

To join the Choir is an opportunity to participate in making great music together with the conductor and your fellow singers, and a expectation to attend the rehearsals and the concerts for the entire season. The Choir’s rehearsal and subscription season runs from late August through early May.

Rehearsals are held each Tuesday evening from 7:30 pm to 10:00 pm at Rodef Shalom Congregation, 4905 Fifth Avenue in Oakland. Rehearsals usually begin the first Tuesday after Labor Day and end in early May following the last scheduled season concert. There are two dress rehearsals, typically the Thursday and Friday evening before each concert weekend, which all members are required to attend. Concerts are typically Saturday evening and Sunday afternoon. A half-day, Saturday choir retreat may also be required during the fall or spring, depending on the difficulty of the music and concert schedule.

Choir members are expected to pay dues to the organization each year. Dues for this season are $195 ($165 for students and seniors [65+]). Dues help cover a small portion of expenses related to music purchase and copying, artistic and administrative staff, liability insurance, and concert venue rental. If paid prior to September 3d there is a $10 discount ($185 and $155). Payment schedules can be arranged and there is a small scholarship pool for those needing help.

Concert dress is a solid black one-piece dress or two-piece top/skirt combination or a black tuxedo with black bowtie and a white shirt.

About the Artistic Director

Thomas W. Douglas

Artistic Director & Conductor

Thomas W. Douglas is a compelling and passionate conducting having performed more than 250 opera, oratorio, orchestral and musical theater productions. He is the Artistic Director of the Bach Choir of Pittsburgh who is regularly receiving accolades for innovative, creative and dramatically provocative productions.  He has also been the music director of the Newton Symphony in Kansas.  Career highlights include conducting Webber’s
Phantom of the Opera
in Basel, Switzerland, Gershwin’s
Porgy and Bess
, the Pittsburgh premiere of the classic silent films
The Passion of Joan of Arc,
with live orchestra and chorus, the U.S. premiere of David Chesky’s
The Agnostic,
the rousing
Camina Burana Africana
, Mozart’s
Die Zauberflöte and Don Giovanni
and a production of
Ain’t Misbehavin
‘ in Malaysia
.

He works regularly as Musical Director at
Music Theater Wichita
where he has done many productions including
Smokey Joe’s Café
,
9 to 5,
and
Ragtime
with Darcie Roberts
Hairspray, The Full Monty, Miss Saigon
,
Beauty and the Beast and Les Misérables
among many others. and has worked with the Anchorage Opera, Pittsburgh’s City Theater, Pittsburgh Festival Opera, Canton Symphony, Wichita Symphony, Dallas Symphony, River City Brass Band and the Pittsburgh Symphony.  He has also conducted classical guitarist and Latin Grammy winner, Berta Rojas and Tony winner, Kelli O’Hara.  Mr. Douglas has been the recipient of the Mary Jane Teall Award and the Robert Frankle awards for his contribution to theatre in Wichita, KS and Pittsburgh, PA.

Thomas has enjoyed the stage roles of Amonasro in Elton John’s
Aida
, Caiaphas in
Jesus Christ Superstar
, Balthazar in
Amahl and the Night Visitors
. He has been a vocal soloist with the River City Brass, Pittsburgh Opera, Pittsburgh Symphony, Canton Symphony, the Children’s Festival Chorus and sings frequently with jazz legend, Joe Negri in his
Mass of Hope
. Mr. Douglas is the Director of Opera Studies and the Director of Choral Activities at Carnegie Mellon University and is thrilled to look forward to future pops concerts with Leslie Odom Jr., Tony winner for his role in
Hamilton
.

Instrument Lending Library

Founded in 1999 by the East Liberty Presbyterian Church,
the Hope Academy of Music and the Arts
was first established to provide high-quality training in music, dance, and theater to families with limited resources. Since then, Hope Academy has remained steadfast in its commitment to creating a diverse and inclusive artistic community that fosters personal and artistic growth.

Chamber Music Pittsburgh is an active partner in advancing Hope Academy’s mission, joining forces with the academy to address systemic barriers to arts participation. Since 2016, CMP has collaborated with the academy to provide a
free, need-based musical instrument lending library.
The library, owned and maintained by Chamber Music Pittsburgh, allows students and families that could otherwise not afford to buy or rent an instrument the opportunity to borrow an instrument to play and learn on. Additionally, participating families receive complimentary tickets to Chamber Music Pittsburgh concerts, further enriching their cultural experience.

ABOUT CHAMBER MUSIC PITTSBURGH

Our mission is to present world-class chamber music ensembles and soloists, promising emerging artists, and innovative programs; and to foster an appreciation for chamber music in the Pittsburgh community by offering educational programs and experiences.

Chamber Music Pittsburgh (CMP) was established in 1961 by a group of civic leaders committed to providing Pittsburgh audiences with the opportunity to hear the world’s finest chamber music artists. Over the past six decades, CMP has continued to realize that vision by presenting an impressive array of the most talented and renowned chamber musicians via its MainStage subscription series, its eclectic Just Summer series, and its Pittsburgh Performs series that features local Pittsburgh artists in unusual venues outside of the traditional concert hall setting.

In carrying out its mandate, CMP has been guided consistently by two basic principles: quality and variety. Each year’s programming is a carefully balanced menu of acclaimed chamber ensembles along with the most brilliant emerging groups. The programs have also reflected a balance of traditional musical masterpieces as well as contemporary, intercultural, and crossover compositions.

Chamber Music Pittsburgh remains a vital element of the cultural life in Pittsburgh and is recognized throughout the classical music world. It is one of the most respected chamber music organizations in North America.

Hip Hop Orchestra from the Hope Academy of Music and the Arts performing at CMP’s 60th Anniversary Gala

Your support makes fulfilling our mission possible! Please consider a donation
via our secure website
, or add a donation to your ticket or subscription order.

Thank you!

Values Statement and Commitment

At Chamber Music Pittsburgh, we believe that equitable access to music and the arts is essential to building a vibrant, just, and inclusive community. We are committed to fostering a culture where every individual—regardless of race, ethnicity, gender identity, age, ability, socioeconomic status, or background—feels welcome, acknowledged, valued, and empowered. We respect the human rights of all.

Music is a universal language that transcends boundaries, fostering connection, understanding, and empathy among individuals and communities. It is a powerful tool for self-expression, shaping personal identity, and unlocking creative potential for all who create and experience it. Chamber music, by its intimate and collaborative nature, unites people across diverse beliefs, experiences, and perspectives. We value diverse perspectives in the creation, presentation and reception of the music we share. As a result, we strive to create a culture of dignity, respect, and belonging for all individuals whom we employ, interact with, and engage, regardless of background or experience.

Guided by the principles of diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility, our Board of Directors, staff, and partners commit to:

Amplify underrepresented voices
in our programming, ensuring that the music we present reflects the rich diversity of our world.

Create welcoming, safe, inclusive spaces and opportunities
for all to engage with chamber music, both on and off the stage.

Cultivate belonging
by actively listening and learning, ensuring that our practices and policies reflect community needs and aspirations.

Champion equity
by addressing systemic inequities within our organization and the broader arts community, and by committing to ongoing education and accountability.

Imani Winds
has led both a revolution and evolution of the wind quintet through their dynamic playing, adventurous programming, imaginative collaborations and outreach endeavors that have inspired audiences of all ages and backgrounds.

MainStage Live

Revolutions: A Radical Returning

We are thrilled to announce Chamber Music Pittsburgh’s 66th
MainStage Live
season!
“Revolutions,” our 2026–27 season, invites you into an exploration of the radical, imaginative, and unique voices in chamber music across four centuries of sound. While our six
MainStage Live
concerts range wildly in theme, genre, and instrumentation, they are united in a
celebration of the artists who have broken boundaries and reinvented themselves time and again.

By turns reflective and passionate, nostalgic and joyful,
this season takes its inspiration from Ludwig van Beethoven,
a revolutionary of his time who helped reshape classical music. Beethoven may be the single best-known classical composer, and the one who has most gripped the public imagination in the 200 years since his death in 1827. The deaf composer who never actually heard much of his music was iconoclastic, strongly principled, and a fierce believer in freedom, shared humanity and democratic ideals – all qualities that resonate with us today.
Beethoven is a lodestar for each of the innovative, world-class artists on our series, and the programs they have crafted, recontextualizating his music for our times, promise to be fascinating, revelatory, and deeply satisfying.

Our 2026–27
MainStage Live
season brings you
six sensational concerts, performed
in our historic home, the resplendent Carnegie Music Hall in Oakland,
and at the adventurous August Wilson African American Cultural Center downtown for one concert.
Join us for a journey through the distinct voices that laid the foundation and continue to innovate this lively art form.

Montgomery Fellowship Quartet

Chamber Music Pittsburgh was founded by Ruth Mitchell Montgomery, who passed away at age 101 in June 2018. Ruth spearheaded the 1961 founding of CMP (formerly the Pittsburgh Chamber Music Society) with the assistance of a Heinz Endowments grant. The
Ruth M. Montgomery Fellowship
was established in May 2000 to honor the contributions she made during her 30-year tenure as Founding Director of Chamber Music Pittsburgh.

Each year, a local high school-aged ensemble is chosen to receive the
Ruth M. Montgomery Fellowship
. The Ruth M. Montgomery String Fellowship Ensemble is selected through an audition process administered and judged by the Pittsburgh Youth Symphony Orchestra. The ensemble receives a year’s coaching in chamber music, complimentary tickets to all CMP concerts, performance opportunities, and occasional master classes with visiting chamber music ensembles.

text:
About CLO

Writing New Chapters in the Pittsburgh CLO Story

Since its earliest days, Pittsburgh CLO has been a forward-thinking organization. In 1946, the idea of producing live musical theater under the stars at Pitt Stadium was a bold undertaking — but driven by the vision that musical theater could bring a community together in celebration of a true American art form, Pittsburgh CLO forged ahead and is now hailed as one of the nation’s premier regional theaters.

With the support of nearly 200,000 patrons each year, the organization continues to produce its critically-acclaimed summer season, launching the careers of
countless performers,
welcoming some of Broadway and Hollywood’s brightest stars to the Pittsburgh stage and defining Pittsburgh as a cultural destination.

However, our mission compels us to do more. Today, Pittsburgh CLO provides year-round entertainment at the
CLO Cabaret
, unparalleled performing arts training at the
Pittsburgh CLO Academy
, valuable
educational opportunities
in the community, recognition for young performers at the
Gene Kelly Awards
, and opportunities for local artists on our stages and work for talented craftsman at the
CLO Construction Center for the Arts
.

And it doesn't end there.

Pittsburgh CLO is committed to ensuring a successful future for the American musical art form by developing
new musicals
and creating new product for regional theaters, Broadway and audiences in Pittsburgh, across the country and around the world. Our involvement in more than 22 Broadway shows as an investor or producer has made it possible for Pittsburgh CLO audiences to see award-winning musicals like
The Addams Family
and
Evita
direct from Broadway on the Pittsburgh CLO stage. In 2014, Pittsburgh CLO stepped onto the world stage with the premiere of a new stage adaptation of
An American in Paris
at the Théatre du Châtelet in Paris, France. An incomparable creative team led by award-winning director and choreographer Christopher Wheeldon made their Broadway debut at The Palace Theatre on April 12, 2015, garnering 12 Tony Award® nominations. This was the first time Pittsburgh CLO has originated a new musical for Broadway.

Our local audiences have also enjoyed multiple world premieres at the CLO Cabaret, and will continue to experience the very latest in musical theater premieres with the addition of Pittsburgh CLO's
SPARK
festival to the organization's efforts.

By taking a leadership role in the development of new works, we are ensuring that local audiences can enjoy the very best of Broadway for generations to come, local artists and students will have countless opportunities to participate in the creation of new musicals and Pittsburgh will be at the epicenter of musical theater innovation.

The world has changed since 1946, but as Pittsburgh CLO has evolved over the years it has never wavered from its mission. Our efforts both on and off stage are all in support of “the celebration” of musical theater and our dedication to our family of supporters who share with us a love for live theater. As we continue to explore opportunities on stage in Pittsburgh, as well as beyond the walls of our theaters and our city, we look forward to continuing to make headlines and musical theater history for the benefit and with the support of our Pittsburgh family.

Mission

The mission of Pittsburgh CLO is the “celebration of musical theater.” Pittsburgh CLO is a not-for-profit cultural organization dedicated to the preservation, creation and promotion of the American musical theater art form, the furnishing of arts education and providing outreach and meaningful community service opportunities in Western Pennsylvania and throughout the United States.

Pittsburgh CLO is a founding member of
The National Alliance for Musical Theatre
and a member of
The Broadway League
.

CLO History

On February 20, 1946, the Civic Light Opera Association held a press luncheon to announce its very first season.
Immediately, talk of a new era in Pittsburgh’s cultural life made a huge splash in all three of the city’s daily newspapers. In fact, the Sun Telegraph predicted that “the CLO will inaugurate a cycle in the city’s musical history that will outlive us all.”

1946
Civic Light Opera premieres at Pitt Stadium

1955
The Civic Light Opera Guild is established

1959
Civic Light Opera moves to the Melody Tent

1962
The Civic Arena is built for the CLO displaying the world’s first retractable roof

1972
Pittsburgh CLO moves to the beautifully renovated Heinz Hall

1985
The Gallery of Heroes program is established

1988
Pittsburgh CLO moves to its current home in the Benedum Center

1989
The doors open at the Pittsburgh CLO Academy of Musical Theater

1991
The premiere of the Gene Kelly Awards for Excellence in High School Musical Theater

1992
A Musical Christmas Carol opens at the Byham Theater

2001
The CLO/CMU New Works Project is established to encourage the development of new works

2004
Pittsburgh CLO introduces year-round entertainment with the opening of the CLO Cabaret

2005
Pittsburgh CLO helps form Elephant Eye Theatricals as a member of 5 Cent Productions

2009
Pittsburgh CLO is co-founder of The National High School Musical Theatre Awards

2010
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 20 years of the Gene Kelly Awards

2011
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 20 years of A Musical Christmas Carol at the Byham Theater

2014
An American in Paris debuts in Paris

2015
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 25 years of the Gene Kelly Awards, 25 years of the CLO Academy, 30 years of Gallery of Heroes. An American in Paris debuts on Broadway

2016
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 25 years of A Musical Christmas Carol at the Byham Theater

2019
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 15 years of the CLO Cabaret

2021
Pittsburgh CLO celebrates 75 years with spectacular performances & events at Heinz Field

A Headshot and resume

text:
Box Office & Ticket Information

Performance dates, times and casts are subject to change.
There are no refunds or exchanges on individual tickets.
Please discuss any special seating needs with the customer service agent at the time your order is placed.

Official Ticketing Websites

PITTSBURGHCLO.ORG
and
www.culturaldistrict.org
are the
OFFICIAL TICKETING PROVIDERS
for Pittsburgh CLO. Tickets from other sources may be: 1) more expensive, 2) invalid and 3) ineligible for assistance. We are not responsible for tickets purchased from other sources.

Tickets purchased from official ticket sources cannot be resold, transferred or distributed to any ticket broker or any other person or entity for resale. Should it come to the Pittsburgh CLO’s attention that a ticket purchaser is a ticket broker, all current and future orders may be cancelled without notice or justification of action. Pittsburgh CLO reserves the right to deny admission to any person with a ticket obtained in violation of these terms.

Puchase Tickets by Phone

To order by phone, please call the Box Office at
412-456-6666
. Tickets can be charged by credit card only. We accept American Express, Visa, MasterCard and Discover. A handling fee is added to the price of each ticket. Tickets will be mailed out until 1 week prior to the show; after that, all tickets will be held at the box office.

Hours of Operation

Days | No Evening Performance | With Evening Performance
Monday - Friday | 9:00 am - 6:00 pm | 9:00 am - Showtime
Saturday | Noon - 4:00 pm | Noon - Showtime
Sunday | Closed | Noon - 4:00 pm (matinee only) Noon - Showtime (evening performance)

Purchase Tickets In Person

Tickets may be purchased in person at the Box Office at Theater Square. The Box Office will accept cash, checks with valid ID, American Express, Visa, MasterCard and Discover.

The Box Office at Theater Square is located at 655 Penn Avenue, near 7th Street.

Theater Square Box Office Hours of Operation

Days | Hours
Monday - Saturday | 9:00 am - 9:00 pm
Sunday | Noon - 6:00 pm

The Benedum Center & Byham Theater Box Offices are only open on performance days, two hours before curtain time through intermission.

Lost Tickets

If you lose your tickets, call 412-456-6666 for reprints. Reprinted tickets will not be mailed but can be picked up at the Box Office. There is a $2.00 per ticket processing charge.

attributes.description: Find answers to some Frequently Asked Questions about tickets to Pittsburgh CLO's Broadway-quality musicals.

text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Are CLO venues accessible?

Each of Pittsburgh CLO's performance venues — Benedum Center, Byham Theater, and Greer Cabaret Theater — are accessible.
Please click HERE for more information.

Are CLO performances appropriate for children?

Pittsburgh CLO is pleased that you are encouraging your children to embrace the wonder and magic of live musical theater! Please note that some shows contain mature content, language, or themes. As a parent, you are the only person qualified to determine what is appropriate for your child. To help you make an informed decision, we encourage you to seek additional information on each show you consider attending. Children under the age of 3 will not be admitted to the theater.
Please click here for our complete Child Policy.

How can I purchase tickets?

Individual tickets to Pittsburgh CLO events can be ordered online, by phone at 412-456-6666, or in person at the Box Office.

What should I do if I lost my tickets?

Call 412-456-6666 and we will make duplicates and hold them at our Box Office for pick-up.

How are the seats numbered in the theaters?

Benedum and Byham seats are numbered sequentially in the Center sections (101, 102, 103...) but in the Left sections the seats are odd numbers and in the Right sections the seats are even numbers. At the Benedum, for example, the Right Center section starts as follows: 22, 24, 26, etc. The Left Center section starts as follows: 21, 23, 25, etc.

What time do theater doors open for a performance?

The doors to the theater lobbies typically open 1 hour prior to curtain. Please refer to your pre-show email for more information about your visit.

Is there a dress code to attend CLO productions?

While many patrons prefer to wear suits and dresses, others dress more casually. Above all, dress comfortably. Consider a sweater or wrap if you tend to be cold.

What is the number for Lost and Found?

Benedum Center: 412-456-2604

Byham Theater: 412-456-1377

Greer Cabaret Theater: 412-325-6766

Are there coat checks?

Coin-operated lockers are available at the Benedum Center. Coat check is available during the winter at the Benedum Center and Byham Theater.

How can I be reached during the show in case of an emergency?

Leave your name, show title and seat location with your contact person. In case of an emergency, they should call the appropriate theater with this information.

Benedum Center: 412-456-2610

Byham Theater: 412-456-2610

Greer Cabaret Theater: 412-325-6766

Do your theaters have elevators?

The Benedum Center elevator is located to the right of the main lobby and accesses all levels.

The Byham Theater elevator is located at the top of the entrance lobby, to the left. Access is provided to the lower lobby (restrooms, coat room and pay phones), and to the top of the balcony only.

Does Pittsburgh CLO donate tickets to area fundraisers?

Yes! Please contact
mail@pittsburghclo.org
to request a ticket donation.

text:
Child Policy

Pittsburgh CLO is pleased that you are encouraging your children to embrace the wonder and magic of live musical theater! To ensure that everyone enjoys the show, below is our policy for children attending CLO performances at the Benedum Center, Byham Theater and Greer Cabaret Theater. We appreciate your cooperation.

Tickets may NOT be purchased for children under the age of 3.

Children under the age of 3 will NOT be admitted to the theater.

No child will be admitted into the theater without a ticket.

Any ticket for a child must be for a seat next to the seat occupied by the adult accompanying the child.

Children must sit in their purchased seat and NOT on the lap of an adult.

Children disturbing the enjoyment of other theater patrons may be removed from the theater at the discretion of the House Manager. NO ticket refund will be given.

Children 12 and younger MUST be accompanied by an adult.

At the Greer Cabaret Theater, guests under the age of 21 must be accompanied by a ticketed chaperone age 25 or older.

Parental Guide
: Some shows contain mature content, language or themes. As a parent, you are the only person qualified to determine what is appropriate for your child. To help you make an informed decision, we encourage you to seek additional information on each show you consider attending. If you still have questions, please
email us.
